Connect to foundations: The classical electron radius and Thomson scattering ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01A magnetic field bends the electron trajectory Besides thermal blackbody emission, nearly light-speed electrons radiate when bent by magnetic fields. This synchrotron emission can appear from radio to X-rays. Use SI units, with electron charge magnitude e and mass me. γ = 1√(1−v²/c²), E = γmec² rL = γmev⊥eB Here γ is the Lorentz factor, not the gas heat-capacity ratio used in the blast-wave chapter. For γ ≫ 1, total and kinetic energies are nearly equal. The pitch angle ψ is between velocity and magnetic field, with v_⊥ = v sinψ. A static magnetic field changes direction but does no work because its force is perpendicular to velocity. Radiation drains electron kinetic energy; sustaining high energies requires acceleration or replenishment. 02Why does the frequency scale as γ²? Define the nonrelativistic gyrofrequency νB = eB/(2πme). A relativistic electron gyrates more slowly, but its radiation is beamed into an angle of order 1/γ. The observer sees only the short interval when the beam points toward them, further shortened by arrival-time compression. For trajectory curvature radius ρcurv, the emission interval is of order ρcurv/(γc), and arrival-time compression adds another factor of order γ². The characteristic angular frequency is therefore of order γ³c/ρcurv. Using ρcurv ≈ γmec/(eB sinψ) gives γ²B sinψ. Radiation theory supplies the exact critical-frequency normalization below. νc = 3eB4πmeγ² sinψ νc ≈ 4.20 Hz × (B1 μG)γ² sinψ 1 μG = 10⁻¹⁰ T. νc is neither a monochromatic line nor the exact maximum of the single-electron Pν spectrum, which is broad and peaks near 0.29νc. The panel shows the νc scale rather than computing the complete single-electron spectrum. 03The Thomson cross section returns Expressing relativistic radiative power through the Thomson cross section σT connects to the foundation lesson. Use magnetic energy density UB. For one pitch angle, P = 2σTcUBγ²(v/c)²sin²ψ; isotropic directions give ⟨sin²ψ⟩ = 2/3. UB = B²2μ₀, ⟨P⟩ = 43σTcUBγ² (γ ≫ 1) This notation does not mean the electron is Thomson-scattering photons here. The same classical charge–mass combination is expressed using σT; the relativistic radiation formula is a physical input. μ₀ is the vacuum permeability. tsyn ≡ E⟨P⟩ = 3mec4σTUBγ ∝ 1B²γ At fixed B, higher-energy electrons cool faster. At a fixed observing frequency, γ ∝ (ν/B)1/2, so the cooling time scales as B−3/2ν−1/2. 04Convert the electron slope to the light spectrum Let the electron number distribution be N(E)dE = C E−sdE. Assume optically thin emission at fixed magnetic field, away from cooling breaks and energy cutoffs. For the derivation, concentrate each electron’s power near a representative frequency ν ∝ BE². jνdν ∝ N(E)P(E)dE jν ∝ E−s × B²E² × 1BE jν ∝ B(s+1)/2ν−(s−1)/2 The Jacobian dν/dE ∝ BE is essential. Define the emissivity slope by jν ∝ ν−α; then α = (s−1)/2. The preceding chapter’s s = 2 gives α = 1/2. Integrating the full single-electron radiation kernel gives the same slope over a sufficiently broad power-law range. Some references define α with the opposite sign. The photon-number index Γ is also different: dNph/dε ∝ ε−Γ gives Γ = α + 1. Distinguish electron index s, emissivity index α, and photon-number index Γ. 05Solve the cooling equation At fixed magnetic field with ultrarelativistic, isotropically distributed electrons, dγ/dt = −aγ². Here a is a positive cooling coefficient used only in this chapter. Separate variables and integrate from the initial value γ₀. a = 4σTUB3mec 1γ(t) − 1γ₀ = at γ(t) = γ₀1+aγ₀t For steady injection Q(E) ∝ E−s, the cooled high-energy steady distribution follows from number conservation in energy space. Neglect escape and let dot E = −bE²: ddE[ĖN(E)] = Q(E), Ė ≡ dEdt = −bE² N(E) = 1bE²∫E∞Q(E′)dE′ ∝ E−(s+1) (s > 1) The electron index steepens by one, so α steepens by one-half. This cooling break assumes constant field, continuous injection, and radiative-loss dominance. An impulsive population or significant escape need not have the same spectrum. 06Return to observations with the assumptions intact Shock acceleration followed by radiation in a magnetic field produces a continuum that gas temperature alone cannot describe. Higher frequencies probe more energetic electrons, which also cool faster. Self-absorption can alter low frequencies, while maximum electron energy and cooling affect high frequencies. Inverse-Compton and adiabatic losses also matter, so a cooling time is not a unique age measurement. The classical formulas here exclude regimes where quantum effects become important. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. At fixed magnetic field, double the electron Lorentz factor. How do characteristic frequency, power, and cooling time change? For an uncooled electron index s = 2, what is the optically thin spectral index α? Show the answer and reasoning In the ultrarelativistic limit, νc ∝ γ², P ∝ γ², and tsyn ∝ γ−1: frequency and power quadruple, while cooling time halves. α = (s−1)/2 = 1/2, giving jν ∝ ν−1/2, away from self-absorption, cooling breaks, and cutoffs.
